fields.h1: Build a Conditional Logic Form That Asks Only What Applies
fields.hero_description: Build a conditional logic form that shows each person only the questions their earlier answers call for.
fields.features_heading: What a Form Can Do With One Answer
fields.features_subheading: Every rule starts from an answer. These six pieces decide what that answer changes on the form and where the response goes next.
fields.feature_1:
Rules typed as plain sentences

Write each rule the way you would explain it to a colleague: if the event is outdoors, ask for a rain date. Emergent builds each condition into the form, along with its database.
fields.feature_2:
Follow-ups that wait for their answer

A question about guests stays hidden until someone says they are bringing one. Respondents get a shorter form, and each response still carries every detail its answers called for.
fields.feature_3:
Whole sections skipped on one answer

One answer can move a respondent past an entire page. A first-time customer never sees the questions about a past order and goes straight to the next section that applies.
fields.feature_4:
Responses sent to whoever handles them

Point each answer at the person or channel that acts on it. A billing question can email the finance inbox while a sales question posts to a Slack channel, both from one form.
fields.feature_5:
A conversation that branches as it goes

Run the form as a conversation that shows one question at a time. The next screen depends on the last answer. Nobody scrolls past a block of questions meant for someone else.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can move to your own repository

On paid plans, export the full code of the form and its rules to your GitHub repository. A developer can read every condition in it and host the form wherever you like.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Forms, Four Kinds of Rule
fields.tab_content_1:
Pick roof repair, and in come three roof questions

Corbel Exteriors quotes roofs and gutters from one form. Choose roof repair and three questions appear: the roof material, its age, and photos of the damage. The gutter questions stay hidden. Ines Varga sends asphalt shingles, 14 years old, with 2 photos, and the estimator reads a request with nothing left to chase.
fields.tab_content_2:
A No on the license question skips two pages

Truck driving jobs at Tollgate Freight start with one question: do you hold a commercial driver's license? Desmond Aguilar answers No. The form skips the two driving history pages and opens the warehouse shift page, where he picks nights. His application saves with the warehouse roles instead of the driver applications.
fields.tab_content_3:
Leaks from any suite post to #building-urgent

Members at Larchmont Coworking report problems on one form, and the category they pick decides who hears about it. A member in suite 304 picks Leak and adds a photo of water under the kitchen sink. The request posts to #building-urgent in Slack. A Wi-Fi problem goes to the IT inbox by email.
fields.tab_content_4:
Under $8,000, it ends with two packages

Halberd Studio takes website inquiries on one form, and the budget answer picks the last page. Under $8,000, the form ends on two fixed-price starter packages. Ravi Castellanos picks $15,000 to $25,000, and his form ends on a page to book a 30-minute call with the founder.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Conditional Logic Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to map the rules of a conditional logic form and test every path before anyone fills it in.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Mark the answers that change it
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write each rule as one sentence
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the questions every respondent sees, whatever they choose: name, contact details, and the reason they came. Keep that core short. Every other question on the form should earn its place by appearing only for the people it applies to.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Go through the core and mark each answer that changes what comes next. A job type, a yes or no answer, a budget range, or a request category are good candidates. Each marked answer becomes the trigger for at least one rule.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write each rule with a trigger and a result: if the order is for delivery, ask for the address. Keeping one rule to a sentence makes two rules that fight over the same question easy to spot before they reach the form.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide which last page each group of respondents sees and who hears about their response. That might be an email to one person for one answer and a post in a team channel for another. Write those down as rules too.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Someone may answer a follow-up, then change the answer that showed it. Decide whether the hidden answer stays in the response or is cleared. Clearing it keeps a response from carrying details that no longer apply to that person.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Paste the core questions and your rule sentences into one prompt. Emergent builds the form with every condition in place, plus the database that stores each response. Read what it built, and add a missing rule with another prompt instead of starting over.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Fill the form once per path
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before you share the link, fill the form once for every path, choosing answers that trigger each rule. Confirm that every follow-up appears when it should and that each test response reaches the person or channel you picked.

faq_plan.q: What is a conditional logic form?
faq_plan.a: A conditional logic form changes as someone fills it in. An answer can show a follow-up question, skip a page, decide who receives the response, or pick the final page. Each rule pairs a trigger with an action, such as asking for a company name only when someone says they are buying for work.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a conditional logic form?
faq_plan.a: Write down the questions, then each rule as a plain sentence, and describe both to Emergent's AI form builder. Emergent builds the form from that prompt, with its logic and a database for the responses. When you find a rule you missed, add it with another prompt and the form changes to match.

faq_plan.q: Which free form builder has the best conditional logic?
faq_plan.ref: Which free form builder has the best conditional logic?

prov.original: Which free form builder has the best conditional logic?

faq_plan.a: No single builder wins for every form: pick the one whose free version handles the rules you need. Tally's help center says conditional logic is available for free to all Tally users. Jotform says conditional logic is available on all Jotform plans, including the free plan.

faq_plan.q: How can I use conditional logic in forms?
faq_plan.ref: How can I use conditional logic in forms?

prov.original: How can I use conditional logic in forms?

faq_plan.a: Use it to show a follow-up only when an answer calls for it, to skip pages that do not apply, and to send each response to the person who handles it. In a multi step form, a rule can also move someone past several steps at once. A rule can change the last page too: a large order can end on a different message than a small one.

faq_plan.q: What are good examples of conditional logic forms?
faq_plan.a: Good conditional logic forms let one answer change the rest of the form. A wedding RSVP asks for a meal choice only from guests who are attending. A support form asks for an order number only when the question is about billing. A rental inquiry skips the pet questions when the applicant has no pets.

faq_plan.q: Can a conditional logic form check a typed answer instead of a multiple choice one?
faq_plan.a: In some form builders, yes. Tally's help center says you can add conditions on any type of input block. Google's help center says going to a section based on an answer is only available for Multiple choice and Dropdown question types. Before you pick one, list the typed answers your rules depend on, such as a number of guests or a ZIP code.

faq_plan.q: Can I put a conditional logic form on a landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent can build the page and the form from one prompt, and a video landing page can end with a short form whose next question depends on the first answer. Keep that form to three or four questions, and let the rules hide anything a viewer does not need to answer.

faq_plan.q: How do I see which path each person took through a conditional logic form?
faq_plan.a: Look at the answers that trigger your rules. Every response from a form built with Emergent is saved with all its answers in a database you own. Filter by the answer that drives a rule, such as everyone who picked delivery, and you have the list of people who took that path.

faq_plan.q: Why is my conditional logic form not working?
faq_plan.a: Check where each rule sits and which question it points at. Tally's help center lists the most common issues: the logic block is placed on the wrong page, conditions reference the wrong field, or the form hasn't been tested with all answer combinations. After you rename an answer option, check every rule that mentions it.

faq_plan.q: Can a conditional logic form change its questions based on where someone came from?
faq_plan.a: Yes, when the link carries that information. Give each source its own link, such as one ending in ?source=booth for a trade show, and write a rule that reads it. Someone who arrives from a qr code landing page can then skip the question about how they heard of you. In Emergent, that rule is one sentence in your prompt.
